task.goal: Make a neighborhood walking route feel welcoming to newcomers without directing people to private homes or making local claims that cannot be checked.
hard_constraints: A community group has one month, a printed map and permission to mark only three public stopping points.
No paid app, GPS tracking, photography of participants or required group meeting.
Route must have a short accessible option and a safe bad-weather fallback; pilot for clarity and exclusion.
task.available_resources: Public-space descriptions and volunteer route inspection.
task.expected_result: A route mechanic and practical pilot.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Three predictable welcomes
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: make the walk welcoming by removing uncertainty. Each of the three permitted public stopping points repeats a simple sequence: ‘You are welcome here,’ one optional observation prompt, and explicit choices to continue, return or finish. There is no task to complete and no implication that regular residents know a correct answer. Predictability could help newcomers feel entitled to pause and explore independently.

The printed map shows a short accessible out-and-back to the first stop and an optional extension through the other two. Volunteers inspect crossings, surfaces, gradients, seating and public access, then describe observable conditions instead of calling the route universally accessible or safe. Directions use public paths and public landmarks; no private homes become destinations. Prompts concern directly observable public features, such as shapes in paving, rather than unverifiable neighborhood history or community attitudes.

For bad weather, the same map offers a seated, no-travel version: follow the printed route diagram and answer equivalent prompts about its symbols and layout wherever the reader is already safely sheltered. A verified, step-free indoor public venue may also be listed, with checked opening hours, but is not required.

Needs: volunteer inspections, one map layout, printing and three authorized signs. Week one checks routes and permissions; week two produces prototypes; week three tests them individually; week four revises and prints. The main assumptions are that a genuinely usable short segment exists and that clear permission language reduces social uncertainty. Welcoming wording cannot repair physical barriers, harassment or inaccessible distribution.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Give six to eight individual testers, including newcomers and people with differing mobility or reading needs, either the prototype or a plain map containing identical route facts. No meeting, tracking or participant photography is needed. Ask them to identify the short option, first stop, return choice and weather fallback; invite an optional accompanied inspection. Collect anonymous notes about confusion, pressure and exclusion. Revise or reject the repeated-welcome mechanism if it adds clutter without improving these decisions or perceived permission to stop. Treat this as a small usability check, not proof of broad inclusion.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Choose your own noticing lens
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: give newcomers authorship over their experience rather than prescribing what they should appreciate. The printed map offers three optional lenses—shapes, words and sounds—with permission to switch, combine or skip them. At each of three marked public stops, a short prompt invites a personal observation. Examples include finding a repeated shape, noticing publicly displayed lettering, or listening briefly without needing to identify a sound. Nothing is scored, submitted or compared with a local answer.

This could make unfamiliar surroundings approachable through curiosity while avoiding claims about local character or history. Every prompt has a non-sensory alternative using the printed map, so hearing, vision, language confidence or current conditions do not determine participation. Avoid prompts involving residents, home details, photographing people or approaching strangers.

Volunteers select three public stops with room to pause without obstructing movement. The first anchors a short accessible out-and-back; the remaining two form an optional extension. The map records inspected surface and crossing conditions, distances and places to turn back. If inspection cannot establish a usable short option, relocate the route before printing.

The safe bad-weather fallback is a seated ‘map noticing’ activity wherever the reader is already safely sheltered: explore shapes, labels and route choices on the sheet without travelling. Clearly advise against starting or continuing during hazardous conditions.

Implementation needs only route inspection, three permitted markers and a folded map. Use the month for inspection, prompt drafting, individual trials and revision. The central uncertainty is whether playful choice feels inviting or childish; offering plain walking directions alongside the prompts protects people who prefer an ordinary walk.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare the lens map with an otherwise identical map offering one fixed observation prompt per stop. Ask six to eight people individually to choose an activity, locate the short route and explain how they would stop or use the weather fallback. Include testers who cannot or prefer not to use one sensory channel. Ask whether the choices increase interest or create work, and whether any prompt feels culturally narrow or patronizing. Drop the lens mechanism if participants repeatedly need explanation, cannot find an equally usable alternative, or prefer the simpler version without losing interest.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A walk you can rehearse on paper
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: reduce the social and navigational cost of entering unfamiliar public space by letting newcomers rehearse the walk before leaving. The printed map contains a three-panel preview, one panel for each authorized public stop. Each panel states what physically marks the stop, where a person can pause without blocking passage, and the next decision. The three actual markers repeat the panel numbers and symbols, making arrival recognizable.

The preview uses only volunteer-checked public-space descriptions: path junctions, public signs, paving changes and other stable features. It contains no invented stories, claims about who belongs locally or directions to private homes. A brief invitation explains that walking alone, taking only the short option and turning back are all complete ways to participate. The intended effect comes from familiarity before arrival, not from completing activities or meeting residents.

The first panel previews a short accessible out-and-back. The longer route adds the other two stops. Volunteers inspect the whole route and publish concrete access conditions, including crossings and surfaces, rather than promising suitability for everyone. If a landmark changes, the panel must still work through a second public cue and a printed distance.

For hazardous weather, the paper rehearsal becomes the complete fallback: trace either route from somewhere already safely sheltered, with no outdoor visit expected. It should be presented honestly as preparation or an alternative activity, not an equivalent physical walk.

Needs are a map designer or volunteer, route inspectors, printing and three authorized markers. Spend the first week checking locations, the second drafting the preview, the third testing it and the fourth correcting it. Its limits are map literacy, changing physical cues and the possibility that extra preview text makes a simple route harder to use.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Give individual newcomers either the preview map or a plain map with the same factual directions. Before departure, ask each to explain the first arrival, short return and weather choice. Offer an optional volunteer-accompanied walk in suitable conditions and note requests for clarification, without GPS or photography. Include seated review by people for whom walking the pilot is unsuitable. The mechanism fails its initial check if previews create false expectations, obscure essential directions or offer no clearer arrival recognition than the plain map. Revise any access description contradicted by inspection or tester experience.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A useful first errand
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: make the route welcoming by helping a newcomer accomplish one small, practical task independently. Instead of asking walkers to appreciate the neighborhood, the printed map helps them locate useful public facilities: for example, a public information board, a public seating area and a publicly accessible drinking fountain. These are examples to inspect, not assumed local amenities. Each of the three authorized stopping points identifies an actual, checked facility and explains how to use or recognize it. Learning where something useful is could give a newcomer a concrete reason to return.

Select facilities that require no purchase, membership, interaction with strangers or disclosure of personal information. Use only public destinations and observable descriptions; avoid claims such as ‘locals’ favorite’ or ‘everyone gathers here.’ Record inspection dates and any opening hours or operating limitations. Do not make an essential need depend on an amenity that may be unavailable.

The first stop anchors a short accessible out-and-back, with two further stops on an optional extension. Volunteers inspect surfaces, gradients, crossings and space to pause, and print specific conditions and distances. Establish a usable short option before finalizing the route. Plain directions remain sufficient; nobody must use a facility or finish an errand.

For hazardous weather, explicitly advise postponing the walk. A no-travel fallback lets readers use the map from somewhere already safely sheltered to locate the facilities and plan a future visit.

Needs: volunteer inspection, a printed map and three permitted markers. Use week one to identify and inspect facilities, week two to draft, week three for individual trials and week four for corrections. The prerequisite is a suitable cluster of public facilities. The main uncertainty is whether practical usefulness feels welcoming; facility failures or narrowly chosen needs could undermine that effect.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Give six to eight individual newcomers either this map or a simple route map with the same destinations and access facts but without the practical-use explanations. Include people with differing mobility and reading needs; offer paper review when walking is unsuitable. Ask each to locate a facility they might use, explain the short return and weather fallback, and identify anything that implies spending, asking permission or needing local knowledge. Optional accompanied walks check whether the facilities work as described, without GPS, participant photography or a group meeting. Reject or revise the mechanism if the explanations add confusion, no destination serves testers’ needs, or access depends on an undisclosed restriction. Treat the result as a small clarity and exclusion check, not evidence of lasting belonging.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A welcome that newcomers help make
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: let newcomers make a small, visible contribution to the route itself. Each of the three authorized public stopping points carries a modest patterned panel with slots for abstract paper tiles cut or folded from the printed map. Anyone may add a tile, rearrange their own tile or simply look. The invitation says, ‘You can help shape this public pattern on your first visit.’ Participation requires no local knowledge, conversation, name or written message. The intended welcome comes from having some agency over a shared object.

Use only supplied geometric designs, with no free-text contributions or claims about who contributed. Never describe the pattern as representing neighborhood opinion or participation counts. Volunteers maintain it as an openly editable artwork. Obtain explicit permission for the panels and their attachments within the three permitted stopping points; this mechanism depends on that permission and basic maintenance capacity.

Place the first panel on a short accessible out-and-back, with an optional extension to the other two. Volunteers inspect public paths, crossings, gradients, surfaces and stopping space, then print distances and concrete access conditions. Relocate the route if a usable short option cannot be established. Panels must be reachable without obstructing passage. Looking is a complete participation option; manipulating paper is never required.

For hazardous weather, advise postponing outdoor travel. The map includes a small version of the pattern to arrange or consider wherever the reader is already safely sheltered.

Within one month, volunteers inspect and secure permission in week one, prototype the map and panels in week two, trial them in week three and revise before printing in week four. Needs include printing, weather-resistant panels, captive tile attachments and maintenance. Uncertainties include whether contributing feels meaningful, whether the panels become cluttered, and whether fine-motor demands undermine the invitation.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Test individually with six to eight newcomers, including people with differing mobility, dexterity and reading needs. Compare an editable panel prototype with the same pattern displayed as a finished artwork, using identical route facts. Ask whether they feel entitled to participate or decline, and have them locate the short return and weather fallback. Offer optional accompanied inspection without tracking or photography. Reject the mechanism if contribution creates obligation, excludes people who cannot handle tiles, or adds no perceived agency over the static version. Check separately that tiles remain secured and panels leave passage clear.

DIRECT_FULL.title: An optional shared challenge with no local experts
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: give strangers to the neighborhood an immediate opportunity to become competent at something together, without needing to meet. The printed map contains a small cooperative-style puzzle whose three pieces appear on the authorized public markers. Each marker supplies an equally necessary piece; no piece depends on neighborhood history, resident knowledge or approaching anyone. Solving reveals a simple abstract arrangement, not a claim about the locality. The potential welcome comes from being equipped to understand and succeed on a first visit.

For example, each marker shows a clearly labeled shape that fits into a three-part diagram on the map. All pieces also appear inside a folded answer panel, explicitly available whenever wanted. The short accessible route reaches the first marker, where a complete one-piece challenge is available; visiting all three offers a different, optional challenge. There are no prizes, rankings, time limits or claims that completing the longer route constitutes fuller participation. Plain walking directions remain visually separate and sufficient.

Volunteers inspect public routes and choose stable public landmarks for navigation. The map records distances, surfaces, gradients, crossings and room to pause. Establish a usable short option before printing, and use only the three permitted markers. The puzzle must work without color discrimination and without requiring reading small symbols; provide a large-print verbal equivalent. Its accessibility remains something to test, not assume.

In hazardous weather, readers should postpone the walk and use the printed pieces to try the whole puzzle wherever they are already safely sheltered. No journey is needed to obtain an answer.

Needs are volunteer inspection, map and puzzle layout, printing and three authorized signs. Allocate one week each to inspection, prototyping, individual trials and revision. The central uncertainty is whether achievable mastery feels welcoming or instead resembles a test; the answer panel and an explicit invitation to skip cannot automatically resolve that concern.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Give six to eight individual newcomers either the puzzle map or an otherwise identical map with the same abstract artwork but no challenge. Include people with differing vision, reading and mobility needs. Ask them to explain the short option, find help or the answer, and identify any implied requirement to finish. Offer an optional accompanied walk in suitable weather, without GPS or participant photography. Drop the puzzle if it obscures navigation, makes people feel judged, or produces no greater sense of confidence than the ordinary map. Revise any format that lacks an independently usable alternative.

EXPAND.title: A walk with a useful destination
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: make the route useful for an ordinary newcomer need. Instead of asking people to appreciate the neighborhood, the printed map helps them find publicly available facilities and understand how to use them. Practical value gives someone a reason to explore independently and may make an unfamiliar area easier to inhabit.

Choose three public stopping points associated with verifiable functions, such as a public information board, seating area or entrance to a public park. These are examples, not assumed local resources. At each authorized marker, state only an inspected fact and one useful instruction: where the public entrance is, where the path continues, or whether the facility has posted hours. Avoid claims about friendliness, popularity or neighborhood identity. No private residence is a destination.

The first useful stop anchors a short accessible out-and-back; the other two form an optional extension. Print inspected distances, surfaces, slopes, crossings and resting opportunities, with the inspection date. Describe barriers explicitly. If volunteers cannot find a usable short segment, relocate the route before printing. Participation requires neither a purchase nor interaction with staff or strangers.

The bad-weather fallback is a printed facilities reference to use wherever the reader is already safely sheltered. It allows planning without suggesting travel during hazardous conditions; it does not promise an indoor venue.

Within one month, volunteers inspect candidate facilities and permissions, draft the map, conduct individual checks, then revise and print three markers and maps. Prerequisites are suitable public facilities and reliable access information. The uncertainty is whether practical usefulness creates welcome or merely provides directions; changing hours and closures also limit reliability.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare the prototype with a plain route map containing the same access and safety information but no facility-use guidance. Ask six individual newcomers to choose a personally useful destination, explain how they would reach it and identify the short return and weather fallback. Offer optional walks in suitable conditions; use anonymous written notes without GPS or photography. Include people with mobility and reading access needs, and provide seated review. Reject the mechanism if nobody finds a relevant use, guidance requires unverified assumptions, or utility information obscures navigation. Any access mismatch requires correction before printing.

EXPAND.title: An anonymous shared choice
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: let newcomers visibly influence a small public artifact. Each of the three permitted stopping points carries a marker with an optional anonymous paper ballot. Participants choose between two proposed titles for that stop’s abstract symbol on the next map edition, or suggest another. The group commits to publishing the resulting symbol titles on a dated replacement sheet at the same three locations. Having a real, bounded decision could create a sense of participation without requiring introductions or local knowledge.

The titles describe printed symbols, not residents, local history or official place names. Clearly label them as temporary walking-map labels. Supply a detachable ballot on the map and a weather-resistant envelope or box incorporated into each authorized marker, subject to permission. No names, contact details, photographs or demographic information are collected. Walking without voting is equally complete. Results describe only submitted ballots, never neighborhood opinion.

The first stop supports a short accessible out-and-back, with reachable ballot access; the remaining stops are optional. Volunteers inspect public access, path conditions, crossings and distances and print concrete findings. All voting locations remain public. If a usable short route cannot be established, relocate it.

In bad weather, participants can make their choice privately on the map wherever they are already safely sheltered, with no obligation to submit it or travel later. The fallback explicitly suspends outdoor participation during hazardous conditions.

Week one establishes permissions and route conditions; week two builds the map and three ballot markers; week three pilots; week four publishes the modest result. This needs printing, pencils, containers and volunteer collection. It depends on permission for these fixtures and the group actually returning results. Sparse participation, vandalism, inaccessible containers or a trivial-feeling choice could undermine the mechanism.
EXPAND.experiment: Prototype one ballot marker and a corresponding ordinary marker without voting. Ask six to eight people individually, including newcomers and people with differing reach, dexterity and literacy needs, to use or decline each version. Check whether they understand what changes, that voting is optional, and that the titles are unofficial. Ask whether the decision feels meaningful or burdensome. Also check short-route and weather instructions. Reject the mechanism if people infer surveillance, official renaming or a required vote, or if the group cannot reliably collect and publish results. Do not treat vote counts as evidence of inclusion.

EXPAND.title: Learn one portable walking skill
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: build newcomers’ confidence through a small, transferable navigation skill. The map teaches one method: before continuing, match the next route instruction to two public cues, such as a path junction and a public sign. The first authorized stop provides a worked example, the second offers a partly completed example, and the third invites an optional independent attempt. Unlike a preview of particular arrivals, the intended benefit is learning a method that remains useful beyond this route.

Keep ordinary directions complete throughout. Nobody must solve a puzzle, pass a test or leave the marked route. Use stable public features inspected by volunteers; never use private homes as cues or destinations. The invitation explains the practical benefit without implying that newcomers lack competence. People who already navigate confidently can simply walk.

The first stop contains the entire worked example and anchors a short accessible out-and-back, so the short option provides a complete experience. The extension supplies practice rather than a required finish. Print distances and inspected surfaces, slopes, crossings and resting opportunities. If no usable accessible segment exists, select another route.

For hazardous weather, provide a small fictional street diagram on the sheet. Readers can practice matching two cues while remaining wherever they are already safely sheltered. Label the diagram as fictional and unrelated to local access conditions. Outdoor travel is unnecessary.

Implementation takes one month: inspect and obtain permissions, draft plain directions and examples, test individually, then revise and print the map and three markers. It requires volunteer route inspection and basic diagram layout. The key assumption is that a brief successful practice improves confidence. Map literacy, visual access and unwanted instructional tone are limits; large print and plain language help but cannot guarantee access for everyone.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare the instructional map with a plain map carrying identical route facts. Ask six individual testers to locate the short option and weather fallback, then interpret one new, simple fictional junction using public cues. Offer an optional suitable-weather walk, recording clarification requests through anonymous notes only. Include newcomers with differing map confidence and access needs; no meeting, GPS or photography is required. Drop the teaching mechanism if it increases confusion or embarrassment, obstructs ordinary navigation, or shows no useful transfer to the new junction. A small successful check supports further testing, not a claim of universal accessibility or confidence gains.

EXPAND.title: Bring a familiar place with you
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: connect an unfamiliar route to a walker’s existing sense of home through optional personal associations. Welcome comes from recognizing that newcomers bring useful experiences and preferences with them. The map invites walkers to make private connections between public spaces here and places they already know; no local knowledge, disclosure or correct answer is needed.

Each of the three authorized public stops offers a different bridge: ‘Think of a public place where you like to pause’; ‘Is there anything here you would also value in that place?’; and ‘What would make this a place you might choose to revisit?’ These are personal reflections, not claims about neighborhood character. Walkers may think, write on their own map or skip every prompt. Include an alternative for anyone who does not want to recall another place: ‘Choose one quality you would want in any public space.’ Nothing is collected or displayed.

Volunteers select public stopping points with space to pause without obstructing others. The first stop carries the complete reflection sequence and anchors a short accessible out-and-back; stops two and three offer an optional extension. Directions use inspected public paths and landmarks, never private homes. Print distances, surfaces, slopes, crossings, resting opportunities and the inspection date. Establish a usable short option before committing to the route.

During hazardous weather, readers can complete the same reflections using the printed public-space descriptions wherever they are already safely sheltered. Explicitly advise postponing outdoor travel.

Use week one for inspection and permissions, week two for the map and three markers, week three for individual trials, and week four for revision and printing. Requirements are basic layout, printing and volunteer time. The central uncertainty is whether personal continuity creates welcome; memories of displacement or loss could instead make the invitation uncomfortable.
EXPAND.experiment: Make two paper prototypes with identical directions and access information: one with the personal-association prompts and one with ordinary route information alone. Ask six to eight volunteers, including newcomers and people with relevant access needs, to try one version independently, with no required group meeting. Across the trials, cover the short route, extension and sheltered fallback. Use anonymous written feedback; take no participant photographs and collect no tracking data. Check whether readers find the short option, understand when to postpone travel, and feel comfortable skipping the prompts. Ask whether the route feels like somewhere they could spend time, and whether any wording assumes a happy former home or pressures disclosure. Misnavigation requires correction regardless of version. If the prompts add discomfort or reading burden without a discernible welcome benefit, drop them. This small pilot can expose failures, not establish a general effect.

A brief invitation explains that walking alone, taking only the short option and turning back are all complete ways to participate. The intended effect comes from familiarity before arrival, not from completing activities or meeting residents.

The first panel previews a short accessible out-and-back. The longer route adds the other two stops. Volunteers inspect the whole route and publish concrete access conditions, including crossings and surfaces, rather than promising suitability for everyone. If a landmark changes, the panel must still work through a second public cue and a printed distance.

For hazardous weather, the paper rehearsal becomes the complete fallback: trace either route from somewhere already safely sheltered, with no outdoor visit expected. It should be presented honestly as preparation or an alternative activity, not an equivalent physical walk.

Needs are a map designer or volunteer, route inspectors, printing and three authorized markers. Spend the first week checking locations, the second drafting the preview, the third testing it and the fourth correcting it. Its limits are map literacy, changing physical cues and the possibility that extra preview text makes a simple route harder to use.
REFINE.experiment: Give individual newcomers either the preview map or a plain map with the same factual directions. Before departure, ask each to explain the first arrival, short return and weather choice. Offer an optional volunteer-accompanied walk in suitable conditions and note requests for clarification, without GPS or photography. Include seated review by people for whom walking the pilot is unsuitable. The mechanism fails its initial check if previews create false expectations, obscure essential directions or offer no clearer arrival recognition than the plain map. Revise any access description contradicted by inspection or tester experience.

REFINE.title: A useful first errand
REFINE.proposal:
Mechanism: make the route welcoming by helping a newcomer accomplish one small, practical task independently. Instead of asking walkers to appreciate the neighborhood, the printed map helps them locate useful public facilities: for example, a public information board, a public seating area and a publicly accessible drinking fountain. These are examples to inspect, not assumed local amenities. Each of the three authorized stopping points identifies an actual, checked facility and explains how to use or recognize it. Learning where something useful is could give a newcomer a concrete reason to return.

Select facilities that require no purchase, membership, interaction with strangers or disclosure of personal information. Use only public destinations and observable descriptions; avoid claims such as ‘locals’ favorite’ or ‘everyone gathers here.’ Record inspection dates and any opening hours or operating limitations. Do not make an essential need depend on an amenity that may be unavailable.

The first stop anchors a short accessible out-and-back, with two further stops on an optional extension. Volunteers inspect surfaces, gradients, crossings and space to pause, and print specific conditions and distances. Establish a usable short option before finalizing the route. Plain directions remain sufficient; nobody must use a facility or finish an errand.

For hazardous weather, explicitly advise postponing the walk. A no-travel fallback lets readers use the map from somewhere already safely sheltered to locate the facilities and plan a future visit.

Needs: volunteer inspection, a printed map and three permitted markers. Use week one to identify and inspect facilities, week two to draft, week three for individual trials and week four for corrections. The prerequisite is a suitable cluster of public facilities. The main uncertainty is whether practical usefulness feels welcoming; facility failures or narrowly chosen needs could undermine that effect.
REFINE.experiment: Give six to eight individual newcomers either this map or a simple route map with the same destinations and access facts but without the practical-use explanations. Include people with differing mobility and reading needs; offer paper review when walking is unsuitable. Ask each to locate a facility they might use, explain the short return and weather fallback, and identify anything that implies spending, asking permission or needing local knowledge. Optional accompanied walks check whether the facilities work as described, without GPS, participant photography or a group meeting. Reject or revise the mechanism if the explanations add confusion, no destination serves testers’ needs, or access depends on an undisclosed restriction. Treat the result as a small clarity and exclusion check, not evidence of lasting belonging.

REFINE.title: Candidate 2 repair: preview the actual arrival
REFINE.proposal:
Original candidate index: 2, “A walk you can rehearse on paper.” It offers the strongest fit: rehearsal can reduce uncertainty using only inspected public-space descriptions, paper and three markers. Exact weakness: naming a landmark and a place to pause does not establish what walkers will encounter from their direction of approach; an accurate preview can still be difficult to match on arrival. Changed action: make each preview an approach-specific, numbered sketch showing the incoming public path, two inspected public cues, the authorized marker and the place to pause. Orient its matching marker diagram the same way. For stop one, explicitly draw the turn back along the short route. This makes rehearsal translate into recognizable arrival and return decisions without adding another activity or mechanism.

Prerequisites: volunteers must inspect each approach and establish a short accessible out-and-back before printing, recording distances, surfaces, gradients and crossings. The other two stops remain an optional extension; all destinations and cues are public, with no private-home directions or unsupported local claims. Within the month, inspect in week one, sketch in week two, pilot in week three and revise in week four. The printed map retains the no-travel paper rehearsal wherever readers are already safely sheltered as the hazardous-weather fallback. No app, tracking, participant photography or group meeting is required. Remaining limit: sketches still depend on usable vision and map interpretation; they must sit beside plain written directions, and inspection cannot guarantee suitability for everyone.
REFINE.experiment: Prototype only the first arrival panel and its matching marker before completing the other two. Ask four to six newcomers individually, including people with differing mobility and reading needs, to identify the approach, pause location and short return using the paper; offer an optional accompanied walk in suitable weather. Ask where either format excludes them or leaves them dependent on help. A wrong approach or return caused by the sketch, or inability to match its cues on site without coaching, falsifies that panel’s readiness: revise it before copying the format to the remaining stops. Also have each tester locate the weather fallback. Use anonymous notes only; this checks clarity and exclusion, not lasting belonging.

SAVE.title: Three predictable welcomes
SAVE.proposal:
Mechanism: make the walk welcoming by removing uncertainty. Each of the three permitted public stopping points repeats a simple sequence: ‘You are welcome here,’ one optional observation prompt, and explicit choices to continue, return or finish. There is no task to complete and no implication that regular residents know a correct answer. Predictability could help newcomers feel entitled to pause and explore independently.

The printed map shows a short accessible out-and-back to the first stop and an optional extension through the other two. Volunteers inspect crossings, surfaces, gradients, seating and public access, then describe observable conditions instead of calling the route universally accessible or safe. Directions use public paths and public landmarks; no private homes become destinations. Prompts concern directly observable public features, such as shapes in paving, rather than unverifiable neighborhood history or community attitudes.

For bad weather, the same map offers a seated, no-travel version: follow the printed route diagram and answer equivalent prompts about its symbols and layout wherever the reader is already safely sheltered. A verified, step-free indoor public venue may also be listed, with checked opening hours, but is not required.

Needs: volunteer inspections, one map layout, printing and three authorized signs. Week one checks routes and permissions; week two produces prototypes; week three tests them individually; week four revises and prints. The main assumptions are that a genuinely usable short segment exists and that clear permission language reduces social uncertainty. Welcoming wording cannot repair physical barriers, harassment or inaccessible distribution.
SAVE.experiment: Give six to eight individual testers, including newcomers and people with differing mobility or reading needs, either the prototype or a plain map containing identical route facts. No meeting, tracking or participant photography is needed. Ask them to identify the short option, first stop, return choice and weather fallback; invite an optional accompanied inspection. Collect anonymous notes about confusion, pressure and exclusion. Revise or reject the repeated-welcome mechanism if it adds clutter without improving these decisions or perceived permission to stop. Treat this as a small usability check, not proof of broad inclusion.

SAVE.title: Choose your own noticing lens
SAVE.proposal:
Mechanism: give newcomers authorship over their experience rather than prescribing what they should appreciate. The printed map offers three optional lenses—shapes, words and sounds—with permission to switch, combine or skip them. At each of three marked public stops, a short prompt invites a personal observation. Examples include finding a repeated shape, noticing publicly displayed lettering, or listening briefly without needing to identify a sound. Nothing is scored, submitted or compared with a local answer.

This could make unfamiliar surroundings approachable through curiosity while avoiding claims about local character or history. Every prompt has a non-sensory alternative using the printed map, so hearing, vision, language confidence or current conditions do not determine participation. Avoid prompts involving residents, home details, photographing people or approaching strangers.

Volunteers select three public stops with room to pause without obstructing movement. The first anchors a short accessible out-and-back; the remaining two form an optional extension. The map records inspected surface and crossing conditions, distances and places to turn back. If inspection cannot establish a usable short option, relocate the route before printing.

The safe bad-weather fallback is a seated ‘map noticing’ activity wherever the reader is already safely sheltered: explore shapes, labels and route choices on the sheet without travelling. Clearly advise against starting or continuing during hazardous conditions.

Implementation needs only route inspection, three permitted markers and a folded map. Use the month for inspection, prompt drafting, individual trials and revision. The central uncertainty is whether playful choice feels inviting or childish; offering plain walking directions alongside the prompts protects people who prefer an ordinary walk.
SAVE.experiment: Compare the lens map with an otherwise identical map offering one fixed observation prompt per stop. Ask six to eight people individually to choose an activity, locate the short route and explain how they would stop or use the weather fallback. Include testers who cannot or prefer not to use one sensory channel. Ask whether the choices increase interest or create work, and whether any prompt feels culturally narrow or patronizing. Drop the lens mechanism if participants repeatedly need explanation, cannot find an equally usable alternative, or prefer the simpler version without losing interest.

SAVE.title: A walk you can rehearse on paper
SAVE.proposal:
Mechanism: reduce the social and navigational cost of entering unfamiliar public space by letting newcomers rehearse the walk before leaving. The printed map contains a three-panel preview, one panel for each authorized public stop. Each panel states what physically marks the stop, where a person can pause without blocking passage, and the next decision. The three actual markers repeat the panel numbers and symbols, making arrival recognizable.

The preview uses only volunteer-checked public-space descriptions: path junctions, public signs, paving changes and other stable features. It contains no invented stories, claims about who belongs locally or directions to private homes. A brief invitation explains that walking alone, taking only the short option and turning back are all complete ways to participate. The intended effect comes from familiarity before arrival, not from completing activities or meeting residents.

The first panel previews a short accessible out-and-back. The longer route adds the other two stops. Volunteers inspect the whole route and publish concrete access conditions, including crossings and surfaces, rather than promising suitability for everyone. If a landmark changes, the panel must still work through a second public cue and a printed distance.

For hazardous weather, the paper rehearsal becomes the complete fallback: trace either route from somewhere already safely sheltered, with no outdoor visit expected. It should be presented honestly as preparation or an alternative activity, not an equivalent physical walk.

Needs are a map designer or volunteer, route inspectors, printing and three authorized markers. Spend the first week checking locations, the second drafting the preview, the third testing it and the fourth correcting it. Its limits are map literacy, changing physical cues and the possibility that extra preview text makes a simple route harder to use.
SAVE.experiment: Give individual newcomers either the preview map or a plain map with the same factual directions. Before departure, ask each to explain the first arrival, short return and weather choice. Offer an optional volunteer-accompanied walk in suitable conditions and note requests for clarification, without GPS or photography. Include seated review by people for whom walking the pilot is unsuitable. The mechanism fails its initial check if previews create false expectations, obscure essential directions or offer no clearer arrival recognition than the plain map. Revise any access description contradicted by inspection or tester experience.

SAVE.title: A walk with a useful destination
SAVE.proposal:
Mechanism: make the route useful for an ordinary newcomer need. Instead of asking people to appreciate the neighborhood, the printed map helps them find publicly available facilities and understand how to use them. Practical value gives someone a reason to explore independently and may make an unfamiliar area easier to inhabit.

Choose three public stopping points associated with verifiable functions, such as a public information board, seating area or entrance to a public park. These are examples, not assumed local resources. At each authorized marker, state only an inspected fact and one useful instruction: where the public entrance is, where the path continues, or whether the facility has posted hours. Avoid claims about friendliness, popularity or neighborhood identity. No private residence is a destination.

The first useful stop anchors a short accessible out-and-back; the other two form an optional extension. Print inspected distances, surfaces, slopes, crossings and resting opportunities, with the inspection date. Describe barriers explicitly. If volunteers cannot find a usable short segment, relocate the route before printing. Participation requires neither a purchase nor interaction with staff or strangers.

The bad-weather fallback is a printed facilities reference to use wherever the reader is already safely sheltered. It allows planning without suggesting travel during hazardous conditions; it does not promise an indoor venue.

Within one month, volunteers inspect candidate facilities and permissions, draft the map, conduct individual checks, then revise and print three markers and maps. Prerequisites are suitable public facilities and reliable access information. The uncertainty is whether practical usefulness creates welcome or merely provides directions; changing hours and closures also limit reliability.
SAVE.experiment: Compare the prototype with a plain route map containing the same access and safety information but no facility-use guidance. Ask six individual newcomers to choose a personally useful destination, explain how they would reach it and identify the short return and weather fallback. Offer optional walks in suitable conditions; use anonymous written notes without GPS or photography. Include people with mobility and reading access needs, and provide seated review. Reject the mechanism if nobody finds a relevant use, guidance requires unverified assumptions, or utility information obscures navigation. Any access mismatch requires correction before printing.

SAVE.title: An anonymous shared choice
SAVE.proposal:
Mechanism: let newcomers visibly influence a small public artifact. Each of the three permitted stopping points carries a marker with an optional anonymous paper ballot. Participants choose between two proposed titles for that stop’s abstract symbol on the next map edition, or suggest another. The group commits to publishing the resulting symbol titles on a dated replacement sheet at the same three locations. Having a real, bounded decision could create a sense of participation without requiring introductions or local knowledge.

The titles describe printed symbols, not residents, local history or official place names. Clearly label them as temporary walking-map labels. Supply a detachable ballot on the map and a weather-resistant envelope or box incorporated into each authorized marker, subject to permission. No names, contact details, photographs or demographic information are collected. Walking without voting is equally complete. Results describe only submitted ballots, never neighborhood opinion.

The first stop supports a short accessible out-and-back, with reachable ballot access; the remaining stops are optional. Volunteers inspect public access, path conditions, crossings and distances and print concrete findings. All voting locations remain public. If a usable short route cannot be established, relocate it.

In bad weather, participants can make their choice privately on the map wherever they are already safely sheltered, with no obligation to submit it or travel later. The fallback explicitly suspends outdoor participation during hazardous conditions.

Week one establishes permissions and route conditions; week two builds the map and three ballot markers; week three pilots; week four publishes the modest result. This needs printing, pencils, containers and volunteer collection. It depends on permission for these fixtures and the group actually returning results. Sparse participation, vandalism, inaccessible containers or a trivial-feeling choice could undermine the mechanism.
SAVE.experiment: Prototype one ballot marker and a corresponding ordinary marker without voting. Ask six to eight people individually, including newcomers and people with differing reach, dexterity and literacy needs, to use or decline each version. Check whether they understand what changes, that voting is optional, and that the titles are unofficial. Ask whether the decision feels meaningful or burdensome. Also check short-route and weather instructions. Reject the mechanism if people infer surveillance, official renaming or a required vote, or if the group cannot reliably collect and publish results. Do not treat vote counts as evidence of inclusion.

SAVE.title: Learn one portable walking skill
SAVE.proposal:
Mechanism: build newcomers’ confidence through a small, transferable navigation skill. The map teaches one method: before continuing, match the next route instruction to two public cues, such as a path junction and a public sign. The first authorized stop provides a worked example, the second offers a partly completed example, and the third invites an optional independent attempt. Unlike a preview of particular arrivals, the intended benefit is learning a method that remains useful beyond this route.

Keep ordinary directions complete throughout. Nobody must solve a puzzle, pass a test or leave the marked route. Use stable public features inspected by volunteers; never use private homes as cues or destinations. The invitation explains the practical benefit without implying that newcomers lack competence. People who already navigate confidently can simply walk.

The first stop contains the entire worked example and anchors a short accessible out-and-back, so the short option provides a complete experience. The extension supplies practice rather than a required finish. Print distances and inspected surfaces, slopes, crossings and resting opportunities. If no usable accessible segment exists, select another route.

For hazardous weather, provide a small fictional street diagram on the sheet. Readers can practice matching two cues while remaining wherever they are already safely sheltered. Label the diagram as fictional and unrelated to local access conditions. Outdoor travel is unnecessary.

Implementation takes one month: inspect and obtain permissions, draft plain directions and examples, test individually, then revise and print the map and three markers. It requires volunteer route inspection and basic diagram layout. The key assumption is that a brief successful practice improves confidence. Map literacy, visual access and unwanted instructional tone are limits; large print and plain language help but cannot guarantee access for everyone.
SAVE.experiment: Compare the instructional map with a plain map carrying identical route facts. Ask six individual testers to locate the short option and weather fallback, then interpret one new, simple fictional junction using public cues. Offer an optional suitable-weather walk, recording clarification requests through anonymous notes only. Include newcomers with differing map confidence and access needs; no meeting, GPS or photography is required. Drop the teaching mechanism if it increases confusion or embarrassment, obstructs ordinary navigation, or shows no useful transfer to the new junction. A small successful check supports further testing, not a claim of universal accessibility or confidence gains.
